1:
Gill offers two placements for the law: either it followed the deaths at once, so that the chapter would stand next to the tenth, or it followed the intervening rules on uncleanness, which were meant to keep defiled worshippers out of the tabernacle. Keil and Delitzsch ground the day in what those daily rites could not do, since many sins would remain unacknowledged and so unexpiated, leaving the congregation with a sense of separation and no true joyousness of access. Ellicott says much the same from the other end, making the chapter an appropriate conclusion to the laws of purification and an annual supplement completing what was daily practised. Henry reads it as directed at Aaron's fear that guilt might cleave to his house, and observes that the atonement made for a family is the establishment of it.

On the warning not to come at all times, Clarke explains that the holy place here means the innermost division, and that entry was restricted to the one day only in ordinary cases. In extraordinary ones, he says, the high priest went in more often — in the wilderness to take down and adjust the furniture at every encampment, and on pressing public occasions to consult the Lord — and Wesley gives the same two exceptions in almost the same words. Calvin puts the restriction down to the danger of familiarity, since a priest entering promiscuously at every sacrifice would have worn away no small part of the reverence due to the place. He adds that a rite seen only once at the year's end represented the one perpetual sacrifice more clearly, while Ellicott traces the later working out of the same care, the Sanhedrin sequestering the high priest for seven days beforehand in a Temple chamber, apart from his wife, lest he contract defilement.

Clarke takes the bullock to cover the high priest, his family, the whole priesthood and probably the Levites, and reads the ram as a token that he and his associates were wholly consecrated to the work. Ellicott adds a detail about ownership: the bullock had to be bought with the priest's own money, because a victim expiating his own sins must be his own property, he needing mercy like the meanest sinner though bound by his office to bring a costlier offering. Wesley notes that what went within was the blood, the body being burnt on the altar outside. Calvin looks past the animals to the office, arguing that a mediator between God and men should be free from every stain, and that since no mortal could supply this a type was substituted, from which believers might learn to expect another.

The plain linen is read as humiliation by Clarke, who points out that the robe, ephod, breastplate and mitre are all absent, so that a man who elsewhere ministers in his dress of dignity here appears before God as a sinner. Wesley agrees, calling it a day not of feasting but of mourning, when ornaments were laid aside. Ellicott treats the four white articles as a fixed class of vestment set against the golden garments, notes that the high priest kept two sets of differing costliness, and reports that the community allowed thirty minae toward them which he might supplement from his own purse. Keil and Delitzsch fix the force of the opening words, that only with these things — the sacrifices, the dress, the washings — could he come in at all.
5:
Henry reports the tradition that the high priest withdrew for seven days beforehand, doing the inferior priests' work himself to get his hand in, and hearing the institution read over to him repeatedly. Ellicott adds that the goats and the ram were bought earlier out of public money, and that under the second Temple the pair had to match in value, size and colour. If one died after the lot fell, a fresh pair was bought, the survivor being fed until ritually defective and then sold for the treasury. Gill insists the bullock was the priest's own, bought at his own expense and not from the congregation's funds, since it expiated his own sin. Ellicott corrects the verb for what he does with it, since he only presents the animal, the killing coming later; Keil and Delitzsch keep the same order, the goats set before the Lord and the lots cast before anything is slain.

Clarke argues that the two goats made a single sacrifice though only one was killed, since no one animal could show both natures of Christ or both his death and his rising, a slain goat not being capable of revival. Wesley divides them the same way, one figuring the passion and the other the resurrection. Calvin describes it as a twofold mode of expiation, one goat offered by the rule of the law and the other sent away as an outcast and offscouring. Gill finds the creature apt on several counts — clean, fit for food, comely in its going — and on one that is not flattering, since something in it is rank and offensive, which suited a surety bearing imputed sin in the likeness of sinful flesh.

Gill sets out the staging from the Mishnah: the priest east of the court and north of the altar, his deputy at his right and the chief of the fathers' house at his left, lots drawn from an urn. Clarke reports that one lot bore the Name the Jews will neither write nor pronounce and the other the word rendered scapegoat, the priest putting both hands in and drawing one in each. Ellicott traces the tablets from box or ebony to gold in the later Temple, and notes the marks that followed, a red thread at one goat's neck and a scarlet on the other's horns. On the disputed word the two part company: Clarke derives it from goat and dismiss, making it the animal sent away, and gathers pagan parallels, chiefly the Egyptian bull whose severed head was loaded with execrations and thrown into the Nile. Ellicott reads it instead as a proper name throughout, and takes the atonement made with the goat to mean atonement made for it, fitting the beast for what it had to do.

The censer, Gill notes from Josephus and the Mishnah, was golden on this day, where on others the coals were lifted with silver. Calvin fixes on the reason given for the covering cloud, that the priest die not, taking it as a sign of how formidable the divine majesty is, fatal to the sight even of the man who serves it. Gill records that the Sadducees held the incense was kindled outside the veil, so that the Sanhedrin's messengers put the high priest on oath in the house where the incense was compounded, not to vary from their instructions. Ellicott has him stay until the place filled with smoke, leave backward with his face to the sanctuary, and pray on emerging that a year meant for drought might be one of rain and that travellers' prayers for fair weather might go unheard. Meanwhile another priest kept the bullock's blood in motion lest it congeal, Gill says, and Ellicott reports the sprinklings counted aloud, one upward and seven downward, lest the priest lose count, Wesley adding that the eastward face signified that he stood there for the people.
15:
Henry follows the priest out to kill the people's goat and back in a third time, sprinkling its blood as he had the bullock's, and explains the object: the people's sins had provoked God to withdraw the tokens of his presence, and this atonement was made so that, being reconciled, he might continue with them. Ellicott fills in the second-Temple practice, the vessel set on a golden stand prepared for the purpose, the goat killed on the north side of the altar, the blood caught in a bowl, and the same posture and counted sprinklings repeated. Wesley takes the occasion to qualify the familiar formula, since the priest entered once a year in the sense of one day in the year, though he went in and came out more than once upon that day. Gill notes that the holy place here means the innermost, as Aben Ezra says, and that although the Targum adds a verbal confession, atonement was made by blood and not by words.

Calvin raises the difficulty that a sanctuary God had consecrated should need cleansing at all, since God remains true though all the world be unholy. His answer is that the place contracted no defilement in itself, yet is justly reckoned unclean in regard to the guilt of the people, and he draws from this that sin is thereby made more exceeding sinful, men profaning the sacred name even while meaning to serve it if they serve carelessly. Keil and Delitzsch ground the same point in the body, holding that the holy things were made unclean not merely by the sins of those who touched them but by the bodily manifestations of a nation's sin, so that they too needed a yearly expiation. Wesley puts it most simply: the people never entered that place, but their sins entered it, and the tabernacle needed cleansing merely for standing in the midst of them.

The clearing of the sanctuary is read four ways. Gill records how complete it was, no priest in the holy place or in any court, and none of the people anywhere. Keil and Delitzsch expressly reject Knobel's reason, that none but the chief servant was worthy to be present, and hold instead that no unholy person should defile by his presence a sanctuary just cleansed. Calvin reads it as a temporary banishment felt as punishment, a melancholy sight when those for whom the tent was pitched had to desert it, teaching them that every part of salvation depends on mercy alone. Ellicott draws a historical consequence from the same solitude: because no one could watch what the priest did inside, the chief priests and the elders swore him on the eve to alter nothing in the traditional ceremonies.

Which altar was then cleansed is genuinely disputed, and Gill lays out both parties. The Mishnah, Jarchi and Ben Gersom take it for the golden altar of incense, which the law elsewhere requires to be atoned for once a year; Aben Ezra thinks it the altar of burnt offering, and Bishop Patrick inclines the same way, reading the priest's going out as a departure from the sanctuary where the golden altar stood. Ellicott follows the second-Temple authorities for the altar of incense and adds the order of the corners, north-east, north-west, south-west, south-east, while Keil and Delitzsch place the rite at the altar in the court. Gill and Ellicott agree on the sprinkling itself, seven times with the right forefinger upon a place swept clear of coals and ashes so that the gold showed, and Ellicott adds that what blood remained was poured out where a pipe carried it away to the Kidron. Wesley closes on the number, seven standing for a perfect cleansing and for a perfect reconciliation by blood.
20:
Henry notes that hands laid on a victim's head were always accompanied by confession, and remarks that although the later synagogue supplied the high priest with a set form, God prescribed none here, a man so acquainted with his people's state needing no words found for him. Ellicott observes that the doubled phrase, both his hands, occurs in no other ceremony, and takes it as the most solemn possible sign that the animal stood for priesthood and laity together, adding that the confession was extempore at first and only formulated later. Clarke works through the three nouns — one from a root meaning to pervert or turn aside, one from a root meaning to rebel, one from a root meaning to miss the mark — which the Jews took to exhaust every breach of the law. Wesley reads the same triple as covering sins of every size, and then makes a claim of his own, that the heathen custom of loading one beast or man with a people's curses was taken from this rite rather than parallel to it.

Gill's point about the sending away is that the goat went where it would never be seen and from whence it would never return. Ellicott renders the phrase literally as a land cut off, meaning ground separated from all around it, a peak or precipice standing by itself, and glosses the wilderness as a place without inhabitants but reckoned the abode of evil spirits. He then marks how far practice diverged from the text, since the law says only that the goat is to be let go, whereas the second-Temple authorities decreed it must be destroyed, a priest leading it some twelve miles to a rock with ten booths built at intervals along the road. Gill meanwhile settles the disputed name against the English version, insisting flatly that the goat and Azazel are two things and not one, and are wrongly confounded in the translation.

Both Gill and Ellicott treat the next verse as describing a fourth entry, made to fetch out the censer and the incense cup left standing between the staves. Gill reports the rabbinic judgment that the whole section stands in order except this verse, and Ellicott confirms from practice that the two acts were performed the other way round, the burnt offerings coming first in the golden garments and the white robes resumed only for this last errand. Wesley presses the point about the clothes, arguing that the garments put on now are the proper high-priestly ones and not the plain linen, which had to be left behind — partly because the meaner attire suited the humbling, and partly because the hands laid on the sin-laden goat had in some sort defiled what he wore. Gill adds where the washing was done, on the roof of a chamber where fine linen was spread for him, and cannot resist the observation that if our Lord was baptized on this day, his baptism being by dipping, type and antitype would answer closely.

The men who disposed of the victims are themselves made unclean. Clarke notes that not only the man who led the goat away but the priest who had consecrated it were reckoned defiled, the animal being unclean as bearing the sins of the whole congregation. Keil and Delitzsch say the same of those who burned the carcases outside the camp, defiled as they were by animals laden with sin, and Ellicott adds that the messenger waited out the day in the last booth, a mile from the city, until sundown. Calvin turns the rule into an argument: when the people saw a man shut out of the camp for merely touching the goat, they were forced to reckon how much wider the alienation must be between God and those whose own sin the creature carried.
29:
Henry begins with the calendar, noting that the seventh month had itself been reckoned the first until the exodus displaced it, and then reports two guesses at what anniversary the tenth day marked. Some have fancied it the day our first parents fell, kept as a fast in memory of the fall; Dr Lightfoot computed instead that it was the day Moses came down the last time with the renewed tables and a face that shone, which would make a day of forgiveness the fittest possible date for a day of atonement. Clarke fixes the day by the reckoning instead, observing that the parallel law calls it the ninth at even because the Jewish day began in the evening, and adding that the jubilee trumpet was sounded on this same tenth day every fiftieth year. Wesley finds a plainer convenience in the season, the fruits being all gathered and the people most at leisure, and takes it as God condescending to their necessities.

Ellicott establishes from the prophets that to afflict the soul means to fast, and complains that the Authorised Version renders the same idiom elsewhere as humbling the soul, so that an English reader cannot see it is one phrase. Wesley divides the affliction between body and mind, abstinence from food and other delights on the one hand and grief for former sins on the other, and insists that the bitterness is voluntary in every true penitent, which is why they are said to afflict themselves rather than to be afflicted. Calvin reads the fast as meant to drive them into more serious penitential meditation without letting them doubt they were truly purged, and insists it worked in a sacramental manner, the outward ceremony being an unmistakable sign of a reconciliation still to come. He adds that the emphasis laid on the priest's office is a eulogy of the coming Mediator, meant to turn the mind of believers to him alone.

What the day covered was already limited in practice. Ellicott notes first that the Hebrew leaves open who makes the atonement, the Lord or the high priest, and prefers the priest; Gill says the word is rightly supplied, following Aben Ezra, since no one else could offer. Ellicott then reports the rule administered in the time of Christ, drawn from the words about being clean before the Lord: only sins against God were covered, wrongs done to a neighbour requiring that the neighbour first be satisfied and his pardon obtained. He adds the sharper half of the same rule, that a man who sins in the expectation of absolution on this day receives none. Keil and Delitzsch draw a different limit, holding that the very need to repeat the atonement yearly showed the sacrifices of the law insufficient to perfect the servant of God in his own conscience.

Ellicott takes the rest commanded here as a sabbath of sabbaths, a day of complete rest, and observes that the doubled phrase is used of the weekly sabbath, this day, and the sabbatical year, but of no other festival. He reports a further consequence drawn from the clause about the anointed successor, that hereditary right to the high priesthood was conditional in a way property is not, the son succeeding only if morally and physically blameless, with the elders judging his fitness. He also marks a translator's inconsistency at the close, the same Hebrew phrase standing three times within four verses and being Englished in two different ways, which hides its force. Gill takes the repetition itself as the point, a law stated three times being one of considerable moment, and reads the closing sentence with the rabbis as saying that Aaron, when the day came, did according to this order.
